# The perseverance of the saints


"My sheep hear my voice, and I know them, and they follow me. I give them eternal
life, and they will never perish, and no one will snatch them out of my hand"
(John 10:27–28). If the grace that saves brings a person to believe, can the one
it saves lose it again? The Westminster Confession of 1647 answers that those
"whom God hath accepted in his Beloved, effectually called and sanctified by his
Spirit, can neither totally nor finally fall away from the state of grace; but
shall certainly persevere therein to the end, and be eternally saved" (XVII.1).
To be *effectually called* is to be called in a way that brings one to faith.
The Synod of Dort had said the same in its Fifth Head of Doctrine in 1619: God
"does not wholly withdraw the Holy Spirit from his own people, even in their
melancholy falls" (V, article 6). This is the *perseverance of the saints*.

## Two claims, and the claim that joins them

Westminster's sentence is about the effectually called, and its tenth chapter
makes them the elect, those God chose to save. Of the elect, Augustine had said
the same about twelve centuries earlier. Those "called according to God's
purpose" are elected, and those who are not to persevere "are not elected" (*On
Rebuke and Grace*, ch. 16). Aquinas says that predestination "most certainly and
infallibly takes effect" (*Summa* I q.23 a.6), and the Formula of Concord that
God placed the elect's salvation "in the almighty hand of our Savior Jesus
Christ, from which no one can pluck us, John 10:28" (Solid Declaration XI.45).
So Augustine, Aquinas and the Lutherans agree with Westminster that the elect
persevere, and divide from it over who the elect are. Trent and Wesley are not
encoded as taking a side on the elect.

Augustine held that some who are truly *regenerate*, given new life by the
Spirit, are not elect: "to some of His own children — whom He has regenerated in
Christ — to whom He has given faith, hope, and love, God does not give
perseverance also" (ch. 18). The Reformed hold the contrary. Everyone truly
justified, that is, put right with God by faith, is among the elect, and those
who fall away never had justifying faith. Among the texts they cite is 1 John
2:19: "They went out from us, but they were not of us; for if they had been of
us, they would have continued with us." Calvin puts it so on Hebrews 6: "God
indeed favours none but the elect alone with the Spirit of regeneration".

So the Reformed conclusion is written as two claims: the elect persevere, and no
one truly justified can finally fall away. A third claim joins them, that the
truly justified are elect. If "the perseverance of the saints" were one claim,
"saints" would have to mean both the elect and everyone truly justified.
Augustine agrees about the first and denies the second, so as one claim he would
seem to contradict Westminster even where he agrees with it.

## The two routes, and where each is disputed

**John 10 and 1 John 2.** From John 10:27–29, the Reformed conclude that the
elect persevere. Calvin reads the verse so: "the salvation of all the elect is
not less certain than the power of God is invincible". Wesley grants the text and
reads its promise as conditional, quoting 2 Peter 1:10: "They are *my sheep*,
that *hear my voice*, that *follow me* in all holiness. And 'if ye do these
things, ye shall never fall'". So the step is rated *disputed*, which means that
a reader the library cites grants its grounds and denies its conclusion. From 1
John 2:19, the Reformed conclude that the truly justified are elect. Augustine
grants the verse and still denies the step: those who left "were not of the
number of children, even when they were in the faith of children" (ch. 20). They
were not elect, and their faith was real. That step is rated *disputed* too.

**Philippians 1.** "He who began a good work in you will bring it to completion
at the day of Jesus Christ" (Philippians 1:6). Trent's chapter on perseverance
first says that "all ought to place and repose a most firm hope in God's help",
and then quotes the verse with a condition: "For God, unless men be themselves
wanting to His grace, as he has begun the good work, so will he perfect it"
(Session VI, ch. 13). So the step from the verse to "no one truly justified can
finally fall away" is rated *disputed*.

The John route reaches the conclusion without Philippians, and the Philippians
route reaches it without 1 John 2:19, though it still needs John 10 for the
elect (`john_strand_establishes`, `philippians_strand_establishes`).

## Augustine, Trent, the Lutherans and Wesley

Four positions hold that one truly justified can finally fall away.

- **Augustine and Aquinas**, on Augustine's ground that some regenerate are not
  given perseverance. They hold that the elect persevere as firmly as
  Westminster does. Augustine's claim, his grant that the elect persevere, and
  the Reformed step from 1 John 2:19 cannot all be held together, and the step
  is where they part (`whereAugustinePartsFromJohnsStrand`).
- **Trent**, from the condition in its chapter 13. Its canon 23 condemns anyone
  who says "that a man once justified can sin no more, nor lose grace, and that
  therefore he that falls and sins was never truly justified". The canon is
  about losing grace; that it can be lost finally is what the condition says.
- **The Lutherans**, from the Formula of Concord. They hold that the elect
  persevere, citing John 10:28, and that some in whom God began the good work
  fall away by their own fault: it "is not as though God were unwilling to
  grant grace for perseverance to those in whom He has begun the good work"
  (Solid Declaration XI.42).
- **Wesley**, from the condition he reads in John 10 and from Hebrews 6:4–6,
  "it is impossible, in the case of those who have once been enlightened … and
  then have fallen away, to restore them again to repentance". He takes it for
  true believers who fell. "The sum of all is this. If the Scriptures are true,
  those who are holy or righteous in the judgment of God himself … may
  nevertheless so fall from God, as to perish everlastingly" (*Serious Thoughts
  upon the Perseverance of the Saints*, §30). The Reformed answer, with Calvin,
  is that those described had "some taste of his grace", a knowledge "which
  afterwards vanishes away", and were never regenerate.

Trent, Wesley and the Lutherans each make the promise hold unless the believer
turns away: Trent "unless men be themselves wanting to His grace", Wesley "if ye
do these things, ye shall never fall", and the Formula of Concord that those who
fall away do so by their own fault. Taken as a condition that can fail, that
simply is the claim that the justified can finally fall away. Taken in the sense
of Dort's Fifth Head, as a condition God keeps in his own sheep ("God is
faithful, who having conferred grace, mercifully confirms and powerfully
preserves them therein, even to the end", V, article 3), it is something Dort
holds. Both senses are checked against Wesley's position, because he has a
second ground besides the condition, Hebrews 6, and his conclusion does not
stand or fall with how the condition is taken (`whatTheConditionMeans`). Wesley
parts from Dort either way. In Dort's sense of the condition he parts at Calvin's
reading of Hebrews 6. In his own sense he parts at the step from John 10, the
step he himself disputes.

## The Remonstrants left it open

The Remonstrants, the Dutch followers of Arminius whose Remonstrance of 1610 the
Synod of Dort answered, did not deny perseverance. Their fifth article says that
Christ, "if only they are ready for the conflict, and desire his help, and are
not inactive, keeps them from falling", so that they cannot be "plucked out of
Christ's hands" (John 10:28). Then it stops: "But whether they are capable,
through negligence, of forsaking again the first beginnings of their life in
Christ … that must be more particularly determined out of the Holy Scripture,
before we ourselves can teach it with the full persuasion of our minds."
Arminius wrote, "I never taught that a true believer can either totally or
finally fall away from the faith, and perish; yet I will not conceal, that there
are passages of Scripture which seem to me to wear this aspect" (*Declaration of
Sentiments*). What the article concludes from John 10:28 leaves the question
open (`remonstrance_leaves_perseverance_open`).

## Weighed together

Weighed as one dispute, Westminster stands off against each of the four
positions that hold the justified can fall away: each defeats the other, so
between them it is a tie. The four do not attack one another. However the ties
are settled, the one thing that must be accepted is what the Remonstrants
concluded from John 10:28: no power from outside snatches believers out of
Christ's hand (`only_the_remonstrance_prevails`). Westminster and each of the
four can be defended, which means each is accepted on at least one way of
settling the ties, and none of the five must be accepted on every way. Every tie
rests on a reading or step rated *disputed*, so the verdict moves only if a new,
cited argument moves one of those ratings.

## What is not encoded

Romans 8:29–30 ("those whom he justified he also glorified") is the third text
most often cited for perseverance, and Hebrews 10:26–29 and 2 Peter 2:20–21 the
texts most often set beside Hebrews 6 against it. None is encoded: no reading
of them was checked against a cited reader with a verified location. Nor is the
certainty of persevering to the end, which Dort grants to believers "according
to the measure of their faith" (V, article 9) and Trent's canon 16 denies except
by special revelation. Nor is falling for a time. Westminster denies that the
elect fall away "totally", and the Smalcald Articles, Luther's articles of 1537,
say that when holy men fall into manifest sins, as David did, "faith and the Holy
Ghost has departed from them". This chapter weighs only falling away finally.
Dort itself grants that believers, left to themselves, "could not persevere in a
state of grace" (V, article 3), and that their falling "with respect to
themselves is not only possible, but would undoubtedly happen" (V, article 8).
The claims here are about what God does, which is where the readers part.

## The positions weighed

Six parties are heard: the Remonstrance, with what it concludes from John 10:28;
Westminster and Dort; Augustine and Aquinas; Trent; the Lutherans; and Wesley.
One position defeats another when it contradicts something the other holds and
its weakest premise or step is rated no lower than the other's. Who defeats whom
is computed from their premises and checked by the kernel.

### Readings

<a id="perseveringReading"></a>
**`perseveringReading`**

The Reformed reading: no one truly justified falls away finally; Hebrews 6
describes those who had only a taste of grace; and no regenerate person is left
without perseverance. The promise is not conditional on anything God does not
himself keep.

```lean
def perseveringReading : Valuation Claim :=
  fun a =>
    match a with
    | Claim.justifiedCanFinallyFallAway => False
    | Claim.hebrews6DescribesBelieversWhoFall => False
    | Claim.someRegenerateNotGivenPerseverance => False
    | Claim.promiseIsConditional => False
    | x => True
```

<a id="fallingAwayReading"></a>
**`fallingAwayReading`**

A reading on which every rival's premises hold: the elect persevere, and some
truly justified, not being elect, finally fall away. Not a position the rivals
share: Wesley, for one, is not encoded as holding that the elect persevere.

```lean
def fallingAwayReading : Valuation Claim :=
  fun a =>
    match a with
    | Claim.justifiedAreElect => False
    | x => True
```

### What follows

<a id="perseveranceReformed_establishes"></a>
**`perseveranceReformed_establishes`**

**The Reformed premises establish the perseverance of the saints**: the
elect persevere, and no one truly justified can finally fall away. That the
second follows rests on readings and steps rated `disputed`: the steps from
John 10 and 1 John 2, and from Philippians 1:6.

```lean
theorem perseveranceReformed_establishes : Establishes perseveranceReformed
-- axioms: propext, Quot.sound
```

**`perseveranceReformed_is_satisfiable`**

theorem perseveranceReformed_is_satisfiable : Satisfiable
    perseveranceReformed.premises
-- axioms: propext, Quot.sound
```

```

<a id="remonstrance_leaves_perseverance_open"></a>
**`remonstrance_leaves_perseverance_open`**

**The Remonstrants' premises leave perseverance open.** Their fifth article
grants from John 10:28 that no one plucks believers out of Christ's hand, and
leaves whether they can fall away by negligence to be "more particularly
determined out of the Holy Scripture". The Reformed reading satisfies it, and so
does a reading on which every rival's premises hold. So the article neither teaches the
perseverance of the saints nor denies it, as Arminius said of himself: "I never
taught that a true believer can either totally or finally fall away from the
faith, and perish".

```lean
theorem remonstrance_leaves_perseverance_open : Independent
    remonstrance.premises (p Claim.justifiedCanFinallyFallAway)
-- axioms: propext, Quot.sound
```

### Where Augustine parts from Westminster

<a id="whereAugustinePartsFromJohnsStrand"></a>
**`whereAugustinePartsFromJohnsStrand`**

**Where Augustine parts from the John strand: at 1 John 2:19.** Augustine
grants that the elect persevere, and the Reformed step from 1 John 2:19 joins
the elect to every one truly justified. Augustine's claim that some regenerate
are not given perseverance, his grant that the elect persevere, and that step
cannot all be held together, and the crux is the step. It is rated `disputed`, and the reader
who disputes it is Augustine himself: those who left "were not of the number of
children, even when they were in the faith of children".

**Why *Reformed, the John strand alone* stands against *Augustine and Aquinas (On Rebuke and Grace; Summa I q.23)*.**

- **The crux:** \\(\href{claims.html#claim-35}{P_{35}} \rightarrow \href{claims.html#claim-42}{P_{42}}\\), a premise of *Reformed, the John strand alone*.
- **What it does:** its conclusion does not follow without it.
- **Granted:** \\(\href{claims.html#claim-35}{P_{35}}\\), \\((\href{claims.html#claim-41}{P_{41}} \land \href{claims.html#claim-42}{P_{42}}) \rightarrow \lnot \href{claims.html#claim-43}{P_{43}}\\), which the break also needs.
- **Where the rival breaks:** \\(\href{claims.html#claim-37}{P_{37}}\\), \\(\href{claims.html#claim-37}{P_{37}} \rightarrow \href{claims.html#claim-43}{P_{43}}\\), \\(\href{claims.html#claim-41}{P_{41}}\\) cannot be held together with \\(\href{claims.html#claim-35}{P_{35}} \rightarrow \href{claims.html#claim-42}{P_{42}}\\) and \\(\href{claims.html#claim-35}{P_{35}}\\), \\((\href{claims.html#claim-41}{P_{41}} \land \href{claims.html#claim-42}{P_{42}}) \rightarrow \lnot \href{claims.html#claim-43}{P_{43}}\\); each is needed for the break, and without the crux they stand.
- **What this rests on:**
  - \\(\href{claims.html#claim-35}{P_{35}}\\) 1 John 2:19 — they went out from us, but they were not of us — *consensus*: 1 John 2:19
  - \\(\href{claims.html#claim-41}{P_{41}}\\) Those God has chosen to save cannot finally fall away from grace — *well supported*: [Westminster Assembly 1647](../../bibliography.md#westminster-confession-1647), §XVII.1; [Schaff 1977](../../bibliography.md#schaff-creeds-christendom-3-1977), p. 636; [Schaff 1977](../../bibliography.md#schaff-creeds-christendom-3-1977), p. 593
  - \\(\href{claims.html#claim-42}{P_{42}}\\) Everyone who is truly justified is among the elect — *disputed*: [Westminster Assembly 1647](../../bibliography.md#westminster-confession-1647), §X.4; [Calvin 1853](../../bibliography.md#calvin-hebrews-1853), pp. 137–138
  - \\(\href{claims.html#claim-43}{P_{43}}\\) One who is truly justified can fall away from grace finally, and perish — *disputed*: [Tanner 1990](../../bibliography.md#tanner-decrees-1990), §Trent, Session VI (1547), canon 23; [Council of Trent 1848](../../bibliography.md#waterworth-trent-1848), p. 47; [Wesley 1827](../../bibliography.md#wesley-works-9-1827), p. 439
  - the step itself — *disputed*: [Wesley 1827](../../bibliography.md#wesley-works-9-1827), pp. 444–445; [Calvin 1847](../../bibliography.md#calvin-commentary-john-1847), pp. 415–416; [Concordia Triglotta 1921](../../bibliography.md#concordia-triglotta-1921), §Solid Declaration XI.45; *disputed*: [Schaff 1887](../../bibliography.md#npnf1-05-1887), pp. 479–480; [Calvin 1853](../../bibliography.md#calvin-hebrews-1853), pp. 137–138; [Tanner 1990](../../bibliography.md#tanner-decrees-1990), §Trent, Session VI (1547), canon 23; [Council of Trent 1848](../../bibliography.md#waterworth-trent-1848), p. 47; *consensus*: [Westminster Assembly 1647](../../bibliography.md#westminster-confession-1647), §XVII.1; [Schaff 1977](../../bibliography.md#schaff-creeds-christendom-3-1977), p. 636

<a id="whereAugustinePartsFromPhilippians"></a>
**`whereAugustinePartsFromPhilippians`**

**Where Augustine's position meets the Philippians route: at its one step.**
Augustine is not cited on Philippians 1:6. The step from the verse to "no one
truly justified can finally fall away" is rated `disputed` because Trent quotes
the verse with its condition, and the Formula of Concord cites it while
explaining why some fall away.

**Why *Reformed, the Philippians strand alone* stands against *Augustine and Aquinas (On Rebuke and Grace; Summa I q.23)*.**

- **The crux:** \\(\href{claims.html#claim-33}{P_{33}} \rightarrow \lnot \href{claims.html#claim-43}{P_{43}}\\), a premise of *Reformed, the Philippians strand alone*.
- **What it does:** its conclusion does not follow without it.
- **Granted:** \\(\href{claims.html#claim-33}{P_{33}}\\), which the break also needs.
- **Where the rival breaks:** \\(\href{claims.html#claim-37}{P_{37}}\\), \\(\href{claims.html#claim-37}{P_{37}} \rightarrow \href{claims.html#claim-43}{P_{43}}\\) cannot be held together with \\(\href{claims.html#claim-33}{P_{33}} \rightarrow \lnot \href{claims.html#claim-43}{P_{43}}\\) and \\(\href{claims.html#claim-33}{P_{33}}\\); each is needed for the break, and without the crux they stand.
- **What this rests on:**
  - \\(\href{claims.html#claim-33}{P_{33}}\\) Philippians 1:6 — he who began a good work in you will bring it to completion — *consensus*: Phil 1:6
  - the step itself — *disputed*: [Wesley 1827](../../bibliography.md#wesley-works-9-1827), pp. 444–445; [Calvin 1847](../../bibliography.md#calvin-commentary-john-1847), pp. 415–416; [Concordia Triglotta 1921](../../bibliography.md#concordia-triglotta-1921), §Solid Declaration XI.45; *disputed*: [Tanner 1990](../../bibliography.md#tanner-decrees-1990), §Trent, Session VI (1547), ch. 13; [Council of Trent 1848](../../bibliography.md#waterworth-trent-1848), p. 40; [Concordia Triglotta 1921](../../bibliography.md#concordia-triglotta-1921), §Solid Declaration XI.42

### What the condition means

<a id="asConditionGodKeeps"></a>
**`asConditionGodKeeps`**

The condition read as one God himself keeps: those who are Christ's sheep do
hear and follow, because God keeps them in faith. Dort's reading.

```lean
def asConditionGodKeeps : Reading Claim :=
  { name := "as a condition God himself keeps in his sheep, Dort's sense",
    commits := p Claim.godKeepsHisSheepInFaith,
    source := asConditionGodKeepsSource }
```

<a id="asConditionThatCanFail"></a>
**`asConditionThatCanFail`**

The condition read as one that can fail: one truly justified can fall away
finally. Wesley's sense.

```lean
def asConditionThatCanFail : Reading Claim :=
  { name := "as a condition that can fail, Wesley's sense",
    commits := p Claim.justifiedCanFinallyFallAway,
    source := asConditionThatCanFailSource }
```

<a id="wesleyAsGodKeeps"></a>
**`wesleyAsGodKeeps`** — Wesley (Serious Thoughts upon the Perseverance of the Saints), read as a condition God himself keeps in his sheep, Dort's sense

Wesley, with the condition read in Dort's sense.

<div class="testimony-derivation">

- (1) \\(\href{claims.html#claim-34}{P_{34}}\\) — Hebrews 6:4–6 — it is impossible to restore again to repentance those once enlightened who have fallen away
- (2) \\(\href{claims.html#claim-40}{P_{40}}\\) — Hebrews 6:4–6 describes true believers who actually fall away
- (3) \\(\href{claims.html#claim-32}{P_{32}}\\) — John 10:27–29 — they will never perish, and no one will snatch them out of my hand
- (4) \\(\href{claims.html#claim-38}{P_{38}}\\) — God's promise to keep those he has begun to save holds unless they fall away by their own fault
- (5) \\((\href{claims.html#claim-34}{P_{34}} \land \href{claims.html#claim-40}{P_{40}}) \rightarrow \href{claims.html#claim-43}{P_{43}}\\)
- (6) \\(\href{claims.html#claim-38}{P_{38}} \rightarrow \href{claims.html#claim-39}{P_{39}}\\) — *would give:* Those who are Christ's sheep do hear and follow, because God keeps them in faith
- \\(\vdash\\) \\(\href{claims.html#claim-43}{P_{43}}\\) — *at issue:* One who is truly justified can fall away from grace finally, and perish

</div>

Grounded in scripture alone: Hebrews 6:4–6 — it is impossible to restore again to repentance those once enlightened who have fallen away, John 10:27–29 — they will never perish, and no one will snatch them out of my hand.

<a id="whereWesleysHebrewsFalls"></a>
**`whereWesleysHebrewsFalls`**

**Why Westminster stands against Wesley, even with the condition read in
Dort's sense.** Wesley's reading of Hebrews 6:4–6 still delivers that one truly
justified can finally fall away. The crux is Calvin's reading of the passage,
that those described had only "some taste of his grace". It is Westminster's
answer to Wesley, rated `disputed`.

**Why *Reformed (Westminster XVII; Dort, Fifth Head)* stands against *Wesley (Serious Thoughts upon the Perseverance of the Saints), read as a condition God himself keeps in his sheep, Dort's sense*.**

- **The crux:** \\(\lnot \href{claims.html#claim-40}{P_{40}}\\), a premise of *Reformed (Westminster XVII; Dort, Fifth Head)*.
- **What it does:** its conclusion follows without it — the crux is its answer to *Wesley (Serious Thoughts upon the Perseverance of the Saints), read as a condition God himself keeps in his sheep, Dort's sense*.
- **Where the rival breaks:** \\(\href{claims.html#claim-40}{P_{40}}\\) cannot be held together with \\(\lnot \href{claims.html#claim-40}{P_{40}}\\); each is needed for the break, and without the crux they stand.
- **What this rests on:**
  - \\(\href{claims.html#claim-40}{P_{40}}\\) Hebrews 6:4–6 describes true believers who actually fall away — *disputed*: [Calvin 1853](../../bibliography.md#calvin-hebrews-1853), pp. 137–138

<a id="whereWesleysConditionFalls"></a>
**`whereWesleysConditionFalls`**

**Why the John route stands against Wesley, with the condition taken as he
means it.** Then the condition says that one truly justified can finally fall
away. The John route needs both its steps to deny that, and the crux is the
step from John 10:27–29, the one Wesley himself disputes (§18).

**Why *Reformed, the John strand alone* stands against *Wesley (Serious Thoughts upon the Perseverance of the Saints), read as a condition that can fail, Wesley's sense*.**

- **The crux:** \\(\href{claims.html#claim-32}{P_{32}} \rightarrow \href{claims.html#claim-41}{P_{41}}\\), a premise of *Reformed, the John strand alone*.
- **What it does:** its conclusion does not follow without it.
- **Granted:** \\(\href{claims.html#claim-32}{P_{32}}\\), \\(\href{claims.html#claim-35}{P_{35}}\\), \\(\href{claims.html#claim-35}{P_{35}} \rightarrow \href{claims.html#claim-42}{P_{42}}\\), \\((\href{claims.html#claim-41}{P_{41}} \land \href{claims.html#claim-42}{P_{42}}) \rightarrow \lnot \href{claims.html#claim-43}{P_{43}}\\), which the break also needs.
- **Where the rival breaks:** \\(\href{claims.html#claim-38}{P_{38}}\\), \\(\href{claims.html#claim-38}{P_{38}} \rightarrow \href{claims.html#claim-43}{P_{43}}\\) cannot be held together with \\(\href{claims.html#claim-32}{P_{32}} \rightarrow \href{claims.html#claim-41}{P_{41}}\\) and \\(\href{claims.html#claim-32}{P_{32}}\\), \\(\href{claims.html#claim-35}{P_{35}}\\), \\(\href{claims.html#claim-35}{P_{35}} \rightarrow \href{claims.html#claim-42}{P_{42}}\\), \\((\href{claims.html#claim-41}{P_{41}} \land \href{claims.html#claim-42}{P_{42}}) \rightarrow \lnot \href{claims.html#claim-43}{P_{43}}\\); each is needed for the break, and without the crux they stand.
- **What this rests on:**
  - \\(\href{claims.html#claim-32}{P_{32}}\\) John 10:27–29 — they will never perish, and no one will snatch them out of my hand — *consensus*: John 10:27-29
  - \\(\href{claims.html#claim-35}{P_{35}}\\) 1 John 2:19 — they went out from us, but they were not of us — *consensus*: 1 John 2:19
  - \\(\href{claims.html#claim-42}{P_{42}}\\) Everyone who is truly justified is among the elect — *disputed*: [Westminster Assembly 1647](../../bibliography.md#westminster-confession-1647), §X.4; [Calvin 1853](../../bibliography.md#calvin-hebrews-1853), pp. 137–138
  - \\(\href{claims.html#claim-41}{P_{41}}\\) Those God has chosen to save cannot finally fall away from grace — *well supported*: [Westminster Assembly 1647](../../bibliography.md#westminster-confession-1647), §XVII.1; [Schaff 1977](../../bibliography.md#schaff-creeds-christendom-3-1977), p. 636; [Schaff 1977](../../bibliography.md#schaff-creeds-christendom-3-1977), p. 593
  - \\(\href{claims.html#claim-43}{P_{43}}\\) One who is truly justified can fall away from grace finally, and perish — *disputed*: [Tanner 1990](../../bibliography.md#tanner-decrees-1990), §Trent, Session VI (1547), canon 23; [Council of Trent 1848](../../bibliography.md#waterworth-trent-1848), p. 47; [Wesley 1827](../../bibliography.md#wesley-works-9-1827), p. 439
  - the step itself — *disputed*: [Wesley 1827](../../bibliography.md#wesley-works-9-1827), pp. 444–445; [Calvin 1847](../../bibliography.md#calvin-commentary-john-1847), pp. 415–416; [Concordia Triglotta 1921](../../bibliography.md#concordia-triglotta-1921), §Solid Declaration XI.45; *disputed*: [Schaff 1887](../../bibliography.md#npnf1-05-1887), pp. 479–480; [Calvin 1853](../../bibliography.md#calvin-hebrews-1853), pp. 137–138; [Tanner 1990](../../bibliography.md#tanner-decrees-1990), §Trent, Session VI (1547), canon 23; [Council of Trent 1848](../../bibliography.md#waterworth-trent-1848), p. 47; *consensus*: [Westminster Assembly 1647](../../bibliography.md#westminster-confession-1647), §XVII.1; [Schaff 1977](../../bibliography.md#schaff-creeds-christendom-3-1977), p. 636

<a id="whatTheConditionMeans"></a>
**`whatTheConditionMeans`**

**What the condition means, read both ways.** The claim is the one Trent,
the Lutherans and Wesley share: God's promise to keep those he has begun to save
holds unless the believer turns away. Both senses are checked against Wesley's
position, because he has a second ground besides the condition, Hebrews 6, so
his conclusion does not stand or fall with how the condition is taken.

Taken as a condition God himself keeps, in the sense of Dort's Fifth Head
(article 3), the condition is something Dort holds. Wesley still cannot be held
with Westminster, because his reading of Hebrews 6:4–6 delivers the falling away
by itself; the crux is Calvin's reading of that passage.

Taken as a condition that can fail, which is how Wesley means it ("a Saint may
fall away"), the condition is the falling away. It cannot be held with the John
route, at the step from John 10:27–29, which Wesley disputes.

Each reading is consistent: Wesley read either way can be held without
contradiction. Both breaks come at readings and steps rated `disputed`, so
neither shows the other side right.

**Every reading of \\(\href{claims.html#claim-38}{P_{38}}\\), answered.** *Wesley (Serious Thoughts upon the Perseverance of the Saints)* holds \\(\href{claims.html#claim-38}{P_{38}}\\). It is read 2 ways here, and each reading is checked; none can be left out.

**1. Read as a condition God himself keeps in his sheep, Dort's sense.** The claim commits *Wesley (Serious Thoughts upon the Perseverance of the Saints)* to \\(\href{claims.html#claim-39}{P_{39}}\\) — so read by [Schaff 1977](../../bibliography.md#schaff-creeds-christendom-3-1977), p. 593; [Calvin 1847](../../bibliography.md#calvin-commentary-john-1847), pp. 415–416 (*disputed*).

Against *Reformed (Westminster XVII; Dort, Fifth Head)*, it cannot be held. Where it breaks:

**Why *Reformed (Westminster XVII; Dort, Fifth Head)* stands against *Wesley (Serious Thoughts upon the Perseverance of the Saints), read as a condition God himself keeps in his sheep, Dort's sense*.**

- **The crux:** \\(\lnot \href{claims.html#claim-40}{P_{40}}\\), a premise of *Reformed (Westminster XVII; Dort, Fifth Head)*.
- **What it does:** its conclusion follows without it — the crux is its answer to *Wesley (Serious Thoughts upon the Perseverance of the Saints), read as a condition God himself keeps in his sheep, Dort's sense*.
- **Where the rival breaks:** \\(\href{claims.html#claim-40}{P_{40}}\\) cannot be held together with \\(\lnot \href{claims.html#claim-40}{P_{40}}\\); each is needed for the break, and without the crux they stand.
- **What this rests on:**
  - \\(\href{claims.html#claim-40}{P_{40}}\\) Hebrews 6:4–6 describes true believers who actually fall away — *disputed*: [Calvin 1853](../../bibliography.md#calvin-hebrews-1853), pp. 137–138

**2. Read as a condition that can fail, Wesley's sense.** The claim commits *Wesley (Serious Thoughts upon the Perseverance of the Saints)* to \\(\href{claims.html#claim-43}{P_{43}}\\) — so read by [Wesley 1827](../../bibliography.md#wesley-works-9-1827), p. 439; [Wesley 1827](../../bibliography.md#wesley-works-9-1827), pp. 444–445 (*disputed*).

Against *Reformed, the John strand alone*, it cannot be held. Where it breaks:

**Why *Reformed, the John strand alone* stands against *Wesley (Serious Thoughts upon the Perseverance of the Saints), read as a condition that can fail, Wesley's sense*.**

- **The crux:** \\(\href{claims.html#claim-32}{P_{32}} \rightarrow \href{claims.html#claim-41}{P_{41}}\\), a premise of *Reformed, the John strand alone*.
- **What it does:** its conclusion does not follow without it.
- **Granted:** \\(\href{claims.html#claim-32}{P_{32}}\\), \\(\href{claims.html#claim-35}{P_{35}}\\), \\(\href{claims.html#claim-35}{P_{35}} \rightarrow \href{claims.html#claim-42}{P_{42}}\\), \\((\href{claims.html#claim-41}{P_{41}} \land \href{claims.html#claim-42}{P_{42}}) \rightarrow \lnot \href{claims.html#claim-43}{P_{43}}\\), which the break also needs.
- **Where the rival breaks:** \\(\href{claims.html#claim-38}{P_{38}}\\), \\(\href{claims.html#claim-38}{P_{38}} \rightarrow \href{claims.html#claim-43}{P_{43}}\\) cannot be held together with \\(\href{claims.html#claim-32}{P_{32}} \rightarrow \href{claims.html#claim-41}{P_{41}}\\) and \\(\href{claims.html#claim-32}{P_{32}}\\), \\(\href{claims.html#claim-35}{P_{35}}\\), \\(\href{claims.html#claim-35}{P_{35}} \rightarrow \href{claims.html#claim-42}{P_{42}}\\), \\((\href{claims.html#claim-41}{P_{41}} \land \href{claims.html#claim-42}{P_{42}}) \rightarrow \lnot \href{claims.html#claim-43}{P_{43}}\\); each is needed for the break, and without the crux they stand.
- **What this rests on:**
  - \\(\href{claims.html#claim-32}{P_{32}}\\) John 10:27–29 — they will never perish, and no one will snatch them out of my hand — *consensus*: John 10:27-29
  - \\(\href{claims.html#claim-35}{P_{35}}\\) 1 John 2:19 — they went out from us, but they were not of us — *consensus*: 1 John 2:19
  - \\(\href{claims.html#claim-42}{P_{42}}\\) Everyone who is truly justified is among the elect — *disputed*: [Westminster Assembly 1647](../../bibliography.md#westminster-confession-1647), §X.4; [Calvin 1853](../../bibliography.md#calvin-hebrews-1853), pp. 137–138
  - \\(\href{claims.html#claim-41}{P_{41}}\\) Those God has chosen to save cannot finally fall away from grace — *well supported*: [Westminster Assembly 1647](../../bibliography.md#westminster-confession-1647), §XVII.1; [Schaff 1977](../../bibliography.md#schaff-creeds-christendom-3-1977), p. 636; [Schaff 1977](../../bibliography.md#schaff-creeds-christendom-3-1977), p. 593
  - \\(\href{claims.html#claim-43}{P_{43}}\\) One who is truly justified can fall away from grace finally, and perish — *disputed*: [Tanner 1990](../../bibliography.md#tanner-decrees-1990), §Trent, Session VI (1547), canon 23; [Council of Trent 1848](../../bibliography.md#waterworth-trent-1848), p. 47; [Wesley 1827](../../bibliography.md#wesley-works-9-1827), p. 439
  - the step itself — *disputed*: [Wesley 1827](../../bibliography.md#wesley-works-9-1827), pp. 444–445; [Calvin 1847](../../bibliography.md#calvin-commentary-john-1847), pp. 415–416; [Concordia Triglotta 1921](../../bibliography.md#concordia-triglotta-1921), §Solid Declaration XI.45; *disputed*: [Schaff 1887](../../bibliography.md#npnf1-05-1887), pp. 479–480; [Calvin 1853](../../bibliography.md#calvin-hebrews-1853), pp. 137–138; [Tanner 1990](../../bibliography.md#tanner-decrees-1990), §Trent, Session VI (1547), canon 23; [Council of Trent 1848](../../bibliography.md#waterworth-trent-1848), p. 47; *consensus*: [Westminster Assembly 1647](../../bibliography.md#westminster-confession-1647), §XVII.1; [Schaff 1977](../../bibliography.md#schaff-creeds-christendom-3-1977), p. 636

<a id="perseveranceNode"></a>
**`perseveranceNode`**

The package each party argues from.

```lean
def perseveranceNode : PerseveranceParty → ArgumentPackage Claim :=
  fun x =>
    match x with
    | PerseveranceParty.remonstrance => remonstrance
    | PerseveranceParty.reformed => perseveranceReformed
    | PerseveranceParty.augustinian => augustinian
    | PerseveranceParty.trent => trentOnPerseverance
    | PerseveranceParty.lutheran => lutheranOnPerseverance
    | PerseveranceParty.wesleyan => wesleyOnPerseverance
```

<a id="perseveranceDispute"></a>
**`perseveranceDispute`**

The dispute over the perseverance of the saints: every party can be held
without contradiction, delivers its conclusion, and has its steps rated.

```lean
def perseveranceDispute : Dispute Claim PerseveranceParty :=
  { node := perseveranceNode,
    consistent := perseveranceDispute._proof_1,
    sound := perseveranceDispute._proof_2,
    rated := perseveranceDispute._proof_9 }
```

<a id="perseveranceDispute_defeats"></a>
**`perseveranceDispute_defeats`**

**Who defeats whom**, all 36 pairs: eight defeats, four standoffs.
Westminster stands off against Augustine and Aquinas, Trent, the Lutherans and
Wesley, over whether one truly justified can finally fall away. The four do
not attack one another, and nothing attacks the Remonstrance. So each of the
four can be defended alongside the other three, and none must be accepted,
because Westminster defeats each of them. Every cell is checked by the
kernel.

```lean
theorem perseveranceDispute_defeats : ∀ (i j : PerseveranceParty),
    perseveranceDispute.defeats i j ↔ (i, j) ∈ [(PerseveranceParty.reformed,
    PerseveranceParty.augustinian), (PerseveranceParty.reformed,
    PerseveranceParty.trent), (PerseveranceParty.reformed,
    PerseveranceParty.lutheran), (PerseveranceParty.reformed,
    PerseveranceParty.wesleyan), (PerseveranceParty.augustinian,
    PerseveranceParty.reformed), (PerseveranceParty.trent,
    PerseveranceParty.reformed), (PerseveranceParty.lutheran,
    PerseveranceParty.reformed), (PerseveranceParty.wesleyan,
    PerseveranceParty.reformed)]
-- axioms: propext, Classical.choice, Quot.sound
```

<a id="remonstranceUnanswered"></a>
**`remonstranceUnanswered`**

How far the dispute is settled before any choice. Nothing attacks the
Remonstrance; every other party has a defeater that the Remonstrance does not
answer.

**What the dispute forces is exactly *Remonstrance (article 5, 1610)*.**

- Stage 1: *Remonstrance (article 5, 1610)*.
  - *Remonstrance (article 5, 1610)* is defeated by nothing.
- Nothing else is forced:
  - *Augustine and Aquinas (On Rebuke and Grace; Summa I q.23)* defeats *Reformed (Westminster XVII; Dort, Fifth Head)*, and nothing forced defeats *Augustine and Aquinas (On Rebuke and Grace; Summa I q.23)*.
  - *Reformed (Westminster XVII; Dort, Fifth Head)* defeats *Augustine and Aquinas (On Rebuke and Grace; Summa I q.23)*, and nothing forced defeats *Reformed (Westminster XVII; Dort, Fifth Head)*.
  - *Reformed (Westminster XVII; Dort, Fifth Head)* defeats *Trent (Session VI, chapter 13 and canon 23)*, and nothing forced defeats *Reformed (Westminster XVII; Dort, Fifth Head)*.
  - *Reformed (Westminster XVII; Dort, Fifth Head)* defeats *Lutheran (the Formula of Concord, XI)*, and nothing forced defeats *Reformed (Westminster XVII; Dort, Fifth Head)*.
  - *Reformed (Westminster XVII; Dort, Fifth Head)* defeats *Wesley (Serious Thoughts upon the Perseverance of the Saints)*, and nothing forced defeats *Reformed (Westminster XVII; Dort, Fifth Head)*.

**What this rests on.** The reasons state 5 defeats and 8 absences of defeat, each a cell of the defeat table, [`perseveranceDispute_defeats`](#perseveranceDispute_defeats), computed from the two parties' premises and checked by the kernel. Whether an attack survives turns on the attacker's weakest link and on the rating of what it attacks, so a changed rating can change the verdict. The weakest links:

- *Remonstrance (article 5, 1610)*, weakest at *consensus*:
  - John 10:27–29 — they will never perish, and no one will snatch them out of my hand — John 10:27-29
  - an inference step — [Schaff 1977](../../bibliography.md#schaff-creeds-christendom-3-1977), pp. 548–549; [Arminius 1825](../../bibliography.md#arminius-works-1-1825), p. 603; [Concordia Triglotta 1921](../../bibliography.md#concordia-triglotta-1921), §Solid Declaration XI.45; [Wesley 1827](../../bibliography.md#wesley-works-9-1827), pp. 444–445
- *Reformed (Westminster XVII; Dort, Fifth Head)*, weakest at *disputed*:
  - Hebrews 6:4–6 describes true believers who actually fall away (encoded as a denial, so it ranks disputed) — [Calvin 1853](../../bibliography.md#calvin-hebrews-1853), pp. 137–138
  - an inference step — [Wesley 1827](../../bibliography.md#wesley-works-9-1827), pp. 444–445; [Calvin 1847](../../bibliography.md#calvin-commentary-john-1847), pp. 415–416; [Concordia Triglotta 1921](../../bibliography.md#concordia-triglotta-1921), §Solid Declaration XI.45
  - an inference step — [Schaff 1887](../../bibliography.md#npnf1-05-1887), pp. 479–480; [Calvin 1853](../../bibliography.md#calvin-hebrews-1853), pp. 137–138; [Tanner 1990](../../bibliography.md#tanner-decrees-1990), §Trent, Session VI (1547), canon 23; [Council of Trent 1848](../../bibliography.md#waterworth-trent-1848), p. 47
  - an inference step — [Tanner 1990](../../bibliography.md#tanner-decrees-1990), §Trent, Session VI (1547), ch. 13; [Council of Trent 1848](../../bibliography.md#waterworth-trent-1848), p. 40; [Concordia Triglotta 1921](../../bibliography.md#concordia-triglotta-1921), §Solid Declaration XI.42
- *Augustine and Aquinas (On Rebuke and Grace; Summa I q.23)*, weakest at *disputed*:
  - To some whom God has regenerated, and given faith, hope and love, he does not give perseverance — [Schaff 1887](../../bibliography.md#npnf1-05-1887), p. 478; [Schaff 1887](../../bibliography.md#npnf1-05-1887), §On Rebuke and Grace, ch. 18
- *Trent (Session VI, chapter 13 and canon 23)*, weakest at *disputed*:
  - God's promise to keep those he has begun to save holds unless they fall away by their own fault — [Tanner 1990](../../bibliography.md#tanner-decrees-1990), §Trent, Session VI (1547), ch. 13; [Council of Trent 1848](../../bibliography.md#waterworth-trent-1848), p. 40
- *Lutheran (the Formula of Concord, XI)*, weakest at *disputed*:
  - God's promise to keep those he has begun to save holds unless they fall away by their own fault — [Concordia Triglotta 1921](../../bibliography.md#concordia-triglotta-1921), §Solid Declaration XI.42
- *Wesley (Serious Thoughts upon the Perseverance of the Saints)*, weakest at *disputed*:
  - Hebrews 6:4–6 describes true believers who actually fall away — [Wesley 1827](../../bibliography.md#wesley-works-9-1827), p. 449
  - God's promise to keep those he has begun to save holds unless they fall away by their own fault — [Wesley 1827](../../bibliography.md#wesley-works-9-1827), pp. 444–445

<a id="only_the_remonstrance_prevails"></a>
**`only_the_remonstrance_prevails`**

**Only what the Remonstrants concluded from John 10:28 prevails: no power
from outside snatches believers out of Christ's hand.** Every other party is
in a tie with another, and this is all that must be accepted however the ties
are settled.

What this does not claim: that the perseverance of the saints is false, or that
one truly justified can finally fall away. Both are in a standoff, and neither
is forced.

```lean
theorem only_the_remonstrance_prevails : Framework.grounded
    perseveranceDispute.defeats = Solver.toSet
    [PerseveranceParty.remonstrance]
-- axioms: propext, Classical.choice, Quot.sound
```

<a id="westminsterDefended"></a>
**`westminsterDefended`**

Why Westminster can be defended: with the Remonstrance, it answers every
attacker itself.

***Reformed (Westminster XVII; Dort, Fifth Head)* is accepted on some resolution.**

- A position holding *Remonstrance (article 5, 1610)*, *Reformed (Westminster XVII; Dort, Fifth Head)* can be held.
- None of *Remonstrance (article 5, 1610)*, *Reformed (Westminster XVII; Dort, Fifth Head)* defeats another, and each attack on them is answered from among them:
  - *Augustine and Aquinas (On Rebuke and Grace; Summa I q.23)* defeats *Reformed (Westminster XVII; Dort, Fifth Head)*, and *Reformed (Westminster XVII; Dort, Fifth Head)* defeats *Augustine and Aquinas (On Rebuke and Grace; Summa I q.23)*.

<a id="perseverance_defensible"></a>
**`perseverance_defensible`**

**Westminster can be defended**: on at least one way of settling the ties,

theorem perseverance_defensible : Framework.CredulouslyAccepted

<a id="westminsterAnsweredByAugustine"></a>
**`westminsterAnsweredByAugustine`**

Why Westminster is not forced: a maximal defensible position holds Augustine
and Aquinas, and they defeat Westminster.

***Reformed (Westminster XVII; Dort, Fifth Head)* is not accepted on every resolution.**

- A position holding *Remonstrance (article 5, 1610)*, *Augustine and Aquinas (On Rebuke and Grace; Summa I q.23)*, *Trent (Session VI, chapter 13 and canon 23)*, *Lutheran (the Formula of Concord, XI)*, *Wesley (Serious Thoughts upon the Perseverance of the Saints)* can be held, and it holds *Augustine and Aquinas (On Rebuke and Grace; Summa I q.23)*; *Augustine and Aquinas (On Rebuke and Grace; Summa I q.23)* conflicts with *Reformed (Westminster XVII; Dort, Fifth Head)*: *Augustine and Aquinas (On Rebuke and Grace; Summa I q.23)* defeats *Reformed (Westminster XVII; Dort, Fifth Head)*, and *Reformed (Westminster XVII; Dort, Fifth Head)* defeats *Augustine and Aquinas (On Rebuke and Grace; Summa I q.23)*.
- None of *Remonstrance (article 5, 1610)*, *Augustine and Aquinas (On Rebuke and Grace; Summa I q.23)*, *Trent (Session VI, chapter 13 and canon 23)*, *Lutheran (the Formula of Concord, XI)*, *Wesley (Serious Thoughts upon the Perseverance of the Saints)* defeats another, and each attack on them is answered from among them:
  - *Reformed (Westminster XVII; Dort, Fifth Head)* defeats *Augustine and Aquinas (On Rebuke and Grace; Summa I q.23)*, and *Augustine and Aquinas (On Rebuke and Grace; Summa I q.23)* defeats *Reformed (Westminster XVII; Dort, Fifth Head)*.
  - *Reformed (Westminster XVII; Dort, Fifth Head)* defeats *Trent (Session VI, chapter 13 and canon 23)*, and *Augustine and Aquinas (On Rebuke and Grace; Summa I q.23)* defeats *Reformed (Westminster XVII; Dort, Fifth Head)*.
